```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 06 - Natural Language Processing](../../Notebooks/Part%2006%20-%20Natural%20Language%20Processing/Part%2006%20-%20Natural%20Language%20Processing.ipynb).
The methods map onto R's tidy text ecosystem: where Python used
scikit-learn vectorizers and VADER, we use
[tidytext](https://www.tidytextmining.com/) (Silge & Robinson) for
tokenization and sentiment lexicons and
[topicmodels](https://cran.r-project.org/package=topicmodels) for LDA.
The analytical questions are identical: what does a corpus of posts talk
about, in what tone, and how would we know if our measurements were wrong?

The previous parts treated posts mostly as *events*: things that happen
at a time, get engagement, and connect accounts. But the posts
themselves are language, and for social scientists language is data.
What are people talking about? How do they feel about it? Do different
communities talk about the same events in different words? These
questions launched an entire subfield when Twitter data became
available: O'Connor *et al.* (2010) famously showed that simple
sentiment counts over tweets tracked consumer-confidence and
presidential-approval polls, and a decade of "text as data" methods
followed.

There are three broad families of automated content analysis, and this
document touches the first two:

1. **Dictionary methods** count words from a curated lexicon. They are
   transparent and fast but inherit every blind spot of their
   dictionary. Python uses **VADER** (Hutto & Gilbert 2014), a sentiment
   lexicon built for social media; R uses the **Bing** lexicon that ships
   with tidytext.
2. **Unsupervised methods** discover structure without labels. Our
   example is **Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)** topic modeling, which
   describes each document as a mixture of word-distribution "topics."
3. **Supervised methods** learn from human-labeled examples. We defer
   these to Part 08, where a large language model plays the role of the
   annotator and we validate it against human judgment.

Whatever the method, the governing principle comes from [Grimmer &
Stewart (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mps028): all quantitative
models of language are wrong, but some are useful, so **validate,
validate, validate**. For more depth, keep that review article open
alongside its book-length successor, [*Text as
Data*](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691207551/text-as-data)
(Grimmer, Roberts, & Stewart 2022), and Silge & Robinson's free [*Text
Mining with R*](https://www.tidytextmining.com/), the tidytext
companion. For the craft of human-coded content analysis that all of
these methods try to automate, Krippendorff's *Content Analysis* is the
standard reference.

### Learning objectives

After working through this document you will be able to:

1. Build a text corpus from author feeds when authenticated search is
   unavailable, reusing the facet-based snowball logic from Part 02.
2. Filter posts by language using the `langs` field on post records, and
   handle posts that declare no language at all.
3. Preprocess short social text (URLs, @-handles, hashtags,
   contractions) with a transparent, inspectable pipeline.
4. Compute word and n-gram frequencies with tidytext and find each
   account's *distinctive* vocabulary with log-odds ratios.
5. Score sentiment with a lexicon, visualize its distribution and monthly
   trend, and articulate its failure modes.
6. Fit and interpret an LDA topic model: top words per topic,
   document-topic mixtures, and topic prevalence by account.
7. Explain when to reach for transformer sentence embeddings instead of
   word counts.
8. Hand-validate automated measures and connect them to the
   LLM-annotation workflow in Part 08.

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
library(tidytext)
library(topicmodels)
```

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. The
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)` line then makes that flag the
default for the whole document: with credentials every chunk runs;
without them the document still knits, but the API chunks are skipped.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)
```

## 1. Building a corpus from author feeds

Every text analysis starts with a **corpus**: a defined collection of
documents. For topical research questions the usual corpus builder is
keyword search,
[`app.bsky.feed.searchPosts`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.searchPosts)
(bskyr's
[`bs_search_posts()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_search_posts.html)),
which Part 02 used to snowball from seed hashtags into a deduplicated
post archive. That remains the workhorse when you are studying a
*topic*. This document demonstrates the other common design: a **panel
corpus** built from the posting histories of a defined set of accounts.
Panel corpora answer account-centric questions (how do *these*
communicators talk?) and are the standard design for studying elites,
organizations, and communities of practice.

### 1.1 A seed account and one snowball wave

Who goes in the panel? We seed with `nytimes.com`, a newsroom whose
@-mentions point to its own sister accounts and journalists, and collect
its ~600 most recent posts. Then we expand the **account set** from the
seed's @-mentions, which live in each post record's `facets` (the
structured annotations marking mentions, links, and hashtags). The
half-dozen accounts it mentions most become the rest of the panel: a
one-wave, mention-based snowball. This is a defensible *demonstration*
corpus, not a defensible *research* corpus: a real project would define
the panel from the research question (all members of a legislature, all
newsrooms in a state), not from one account's conversational orbit. The
boundary-specification worries from Part 03 apply to corpora too.

We reuse Part 02's design in miniature: collect the seed's posts, find
the accounts it mentions most, and add their posts to form a small
*panel corpus*. The fetcher below should look familiar by now — it calls
[`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html), drops
reposts, pull `text`, `created_at`, `langs`, and `facets` out of the
`record` list-column — with `transmute()` (a `mutate()` that keeps only
the columns it names) producing exactly the tidy frame the rest of the
pipeline needs. `is_repost()` is one of the small helpers defined in
`bsky_client.R`: it reads bskyr's `` reason_$type `` column and returns
`TRUE` for reposts (and `FALSE` for pinned posts, which carry a
different marker), so the corpus holds only the authors' own words:

```{r corpus-seed}
SEED_ACCOUNT <- "nytimes.com"
COLLECTED_ON <- format(today(), "%Y-%m-%d")

fetch_posts <- function(actor, max_posts) {
  feed <- bs_get_author_feed(actor, limit = max_posts)
  feed |>
    filter(!is_repost(feed)) |>   # helper from bsky_client.R
    transmute(
      uri,
      author = author_handle,
      created_at = map_chr(record, "created_at", .default = NA),
      text = map_chr(record, "text", .default = ""),
      langs = map(record, \(r) unlist(r$langs)),
      facets = map(record, \(r) r$facets[[1]])
    )
}

seed_posts <- fetch_posts(SEED_ACCOUNT, 600)

c(posts = nrow(seed_posts), collected_on = COLLECTED_ON,
  earliest = min(seed_posts$created_at), latest = max(seed_posts$created_at))
```

`COLLECTED_ON` records the collection date, a series convention from
Part 01: a corpus is a *snapshot*, and anyone re-knitting this document
later will collect different posts, so the date travels with the
archive's metadata (Section 8). The date range shows how far back ~600
posts reaches for this account: posting rate determines the window, a
composition fact that matters when we plot trends over time in Section
4.1.

Next, the one-wave snowball. The nested `map()` calls walk the facet
structure exactly as in Part 02 (facets → features → mention DIDs);
`table()` tallies how often each account is mentioned;
[`bs_get_profile()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_profile.html) looks up the
most-mentioned accounts; and we keep the six that actually have posts. Two defensive
habits from Part 02 appear here. We fetch each account by its DID rather
than its handle, because a handle can stop working (when its domain
lapses, Bluesky shows it as `handle.invalid`) while the DID stays
valid. And `tryCatch()` skips any account the API refuses, such as one
deleted since it was mentioned, with a message rather than stopping the
whole collection:

```{r corpus-panel}
mention_dids <- seed_posts$facets |>
  map(\(facets) {
    map(facets, \(facet) {
      map_chr(facet$features, \(f) {
        if (endsWith(f$`$type`, "#mention")) f$did else NA_character_
      })
    })
  }) |>
  unlist() |>
  discard(is.na)

c(mentions = length(mention_dids), distinct_accounts = n_distinct(mention_dids))

top_mentioned <- head(names(sort(table(mention_dids), decreasing = TRUE)), 8)
profiles <- bs_get_profile(top_mentioned)
panel_dids <- profiles |>
  filter(posts_count > 0) |>
  slice_head(n = 6) |>
  pull(did)

panel_posts <- map(panel_dids, \(did) {
  out <- tryCatch(fetch_posts(did, 150), error = \(e) {
    message("Skipping ", did, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
    NULL
  })
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
  out
}) |> list_rbind()

c(seed = nrow(seed_posts), panel = nrow(panel_posts))
```

With the 600-post seed and at most six panel accounts at 150 posts each,
the corpus is capped at about 1,500 posts: plenty for a tutorial, small
enough to stay polite.

### 1.2 Tidying and filtering by language

Every method below (English stopwords, an English sentiment lexicon, a
bag-of-words topic model) assumes English text. Post records carry a
self-declared `langs` field set by the posting client, which is
imperfect in two different ways. It can be **wrong**: clients usually
fill it in from the device's language settings. And it can be **empty**:
some clients, including the publishing tools many newsrooms use, record
no language at all. An empty `langs` is *missing data*. It tells us
nothing about the post's language, so a filter that keeps only posts that
*declare* English quietly treats "no answer" as "not English".

Our `language_status()` function sorts each post into one of four
groups instead:

| Group | Meaning |
|---|---|
| declared English | `langs` includes an English tag |
| declared other | `langs` names only other languages |
| undeclared, looks English | `langs` is empty, but the text passes a simple English test |
| undeclared, not English or too short | `langs` is empty and the test fails or can't tell |

The simple test counts **function words**, the short grammatical words
("the", "of", "and", "with") that make up a large share of any English
sentence but almost never appear in Spanish, French, Portuguese, or
German. If at least 10% of a post's words are English function words we
call it English; posts with fewer than five words are too short to judge.
It is the same crude, transparent rule the Python notebook uses, one you
can check by reading posts. (The regular expression `[^\W\d_]+`
used with `str_extract_all()` matches runs of letters in any alphabet.)

```{r language-status}
ENGLISH_FUNCTION_WORDS <- c(
  "the", "and", "of", "to", "is", "for", "that", "with", "on", "was",
  "are", "this", "it", "from", "by", "at", "as", "be", "has", "have", "an",
  "his", "her", "their", "they", "after", "about", "who", "will", "what",
  "more", "said", "its", "were", "been", "than", "which", "not", "but",
  "or", "how", "why", "when", "new")

# Patterns shared with the tokenizer in Section 2
URL_PATTERN <- "https?://\\S+|www\\.\\S+"
HANDLE_PATTERN <- "@[A-Za-z0-9.\\-]+"
# Display URLs like "nytimes.com/2026/11/..." (each dotted part >= 2 chars,
# so "e.g." and "U.S." survive)
DISPLAY_URL_PATTERN <- "\\b\\w[\\w\\-]*(?:\\.[\\w\\-]{2,})+(?:/\\S*)?"

strip_links <- function(text) {
  text |>
    str_remove_all(URL_PATTERN) |>
    str_remove_all(HANDLE_PATTERN) |>
    str_remove_all(DISPLAY_URL_PATTERN)
}

language_status <- function(langs, text, threshold = 0.10, min_words = 5) {
  map2_chr(langs, text, \(l, t) {
    l <- as.character(unlist(l))
    if (any(startsWith(tolower(l), "en"))) return("declared English")
    if (length(l) > 0) return("declared other")
    words <- str_extract_all(strip_links(str_to_lower(t)), "[^\\W\\d_]+")[[1]]
    if (length(words) >= min_words &&
        mean(words %in% ENGLISH_FUNCTION_WORDS) >= threshold) {
      return("undeclared, looks English")
    }
    "undeclared, not English or too short"
  })
}
```

Now de-duplicate by URI, classify every post, and look at the result
*before* filtering. `count()` tallies posts per account and group, and
`pivot_wider()` spreads the groups into columns:

```{r corpus-tidy}
corpus_all <- bind_rows(seed_posts, panel_posts) |>
  distinct(uri, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(created_at = ymd_hms(created_at, quiet = TRUE),
         language_status = language_status(langs, text))

corpus_all |>
  count(author, language_status) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = language_status, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

Read the table row by row. For the newsroom accounts, most posts
typically land in an *undeclared* column, because their publishing tools
never fill in `langs`; the individual journalists who post from the
Bluesky app usually declare English. Had we kept only declared-English
posts, the corpus would have lost most of exactly the institutional
accounts the design is about. The general lesson: **self-reported
metadata is missing in a way that is not random**, so check who is
missing before you filter on it.

Now apply the rule — keep posts that declare English, or declare nothing
but pass the test, and that have non-empty text:

```{r corpus-filter}
corpus <- corpus_all |>
  filter(language_status %in% c("declared English", "undeclared, looks English"),
         str_squish(text) != "") |>
  select(uri, author, created_at, text, language_status)

corpus |> count(author, sort = TRUE)
```

## 2. Preprocessing short social text

Counting words sounds trivial until you look at an actual post. Social
media text is short (Bluesky caps posts at 300 graphemes), dense with
platform syntax (URLs, @-handles that are *domain names* on Bluesky,
#hashtags), and full of contractions, emoji, and creative spelling.
Every preprocessing choice changes what your model can see.

Two terms of art first. A **token** is the basic unit text gets chopped
into for counting (here, lowercase words), and **tokenization** is the
deceptively consequential act of chopping: is `#DataScience` one token
or two? A **stopword** is a word so common and so topically empty (*the*,
*and*, *of*, *is*) that we delete it before counting, on the theory that
it says nothing about what a post is *about*. Both come with judgment
calls: *not* sits on many stopword lists, and dropping it destroys
negation.

Before tokenizing, we strip links and handles with the `strip_links()`
helper from Section 1.2. That includes **display URLs**: Bluesky clients
show links without the `https://` (for example
`nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/...`), and without this step `unnest_tokens()`
would split each one into junk tokens like `nytimes`, `com`, and `2026`.
We also turn `#hashtag` into the plain word `hashtag`, because the tag
is content. `unnest_tokens()` then lowercases and splits on word
boundaries, and we remove stopwords. Custom stopwords matter on social
text, where some short artifacts are frequent but meaningless:

```{r tokens}
custom_stop <- tibble(word = c("amp", "gt", "lt", "via"))

clean_text <- function(text) {
  text |>
    str_to_lower() |>
    strip_links() |>
    str_replace_all("#", " ")
}

tokens <- corpus |>
  mutate(text_clean = clean_text(text)) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text_clean) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  anti_join(custom_stop, by = "word") |>
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z]"))

c(posts = n_distinct(tokens$uri), tokens = nrow(tokens),
  vocabulary = n_distinct(tokens$word))
```

### What did we just throw away?

Be honest about the costs before celebrating the clean tokens:

* **Emoji and emoticons** often carry the entire sentiment of a short
  post ("great. 🙄"). Our tokenizer keeps only letters, so they vanish.
* **Sarcasm and irony** survive preprocessing but defeat every
  bag-of-words method, since they depend on context no word list
  encodes.
* **Multilinguality**: an English-only filter plus English stopwords
  means code-switching posts are mangled and non-English voices are
  excluded entirely.
* **Word order and negation**: "the protest stopped the violence" and
  "the violence stopped the protest" become identical bags of words, and
  stopword lists often delete "not".

None of these are reasons not to proceed; they are reasons to *validate*
whatever we compute downstream. Print a before/after pair whenever you
change the pipeline, and keep the raw `text` column forever:

```{r before-after}
example <- corpus |> filter(author == SEED_ACCOUNT) |>
  slice_head(n = 1)
example$text
tokens |> filter(uri == example$uri) |> pull(word)
```

## 3. Word and n-gram frequencies

The simplest content analysis is a word count. An **n-gram** is a run
of *n* adjacent tokens: a **unigram** is a single word, a **bigram** an
adjacent pair, and so on. Counting n-grams is the workhorse of every
"bag-of-words" analysis, so called because it treats a document as an
unordered bag of tokens. Bigrams (built by `unnest_tokens()` with
`token = "ngrams", n = 2`) recover a little of the word order we
destroyed, surfacing names and phrases that unigrams split apart, like
"new york". One refinement you will meet constantly is **tf-idf** (term
frequency–inverse document frequency), which down-weights words that
appear in *many* documents; tidytext's `bind_tf_idf()` computes it. We
stay with raw counts, because they are directly readable and the LDA
model in Section 5 is defined over counts. `reorder_within()` sorts the
bars within each facet:

```{r frequencies, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
unigrams <- tokens |> count(word, sort = TRUE)

bigrams <- corpus |>
  mutate(text_clean = clean_text(text)) |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text_clean, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  separate(bigram, c("w1", "w2"), sep = " ") |>
  filter(!w1 %in% stop_words$word, !w2 %in% stop_words$word) |>
  unite(bigram, w1, w2, sep = " ") |>
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)

bind_rows(
  unigrams |> slice_head(n = 20) |> transmute(term = word, n, kind = "unigrams"),
  bigrams |> slice_head(n = 20) |> transmute(term = bigram, n, kind = "bigrams")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, reorder_within(term, n, kind))) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = kind), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  facet_wrap(~kind, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Occurrences in corpus", y = NULL,
       title = paste("Most frequent terms across", nrow(corpus), "posts")) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Notice how much more *interpretable* the bigrams tend to be: a two-word
place name or a person's full name tells you something that a lone
"new" does not. That interpretability gain is why n-grams are worth their
cost (a much larger, sparser vocabulary).

### 3.1 What makes each account distinctive?

Raw frequency rewards verbosity: the seed account posts the most, so it
dominates every top-words list. *Log-odds ratios* fix this by comparing
each account's rate of using a word against everyone else's rate of
using it — a word scores high for an account when that account uses it
disproportionately, not merely often. The +0.5 *smoothing* keeps words
one group never uses from producing log(0):

```{r log-odds}
account_words <- tokens |> count(author, word)

distinctive <- account_words |>
  group_by(word) |>
  mutate(total = sum(n)) |>
  group_by(author) |>
  mutate(
    own_total = sum(n),
    rest = total - n,
    rest_total = sum(account_words$n) - own_total,
    log_odds = log((n + 0.5) / (own_total - n + 0.5)) -
               log((rest + 0.5) / (rest_total - rest + 0.5))
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 3) |>
  slice_max(log_odds, n = 8) |>
  summarise(distinctive_words = paste(word, collapse = ", "),
            .groups = "drop")

distinctive
```

Each row should read like a thumbnail sketch of an account's beat: the
opinion columnists' moral and political vocabulary, the newsroom's place
names and breaking-news words, the sports accounts' teams and leagues.
That is exactly the kind of *face validity check* Grimmer & Stewart
prescribe: before trusting any statistic, look at whether the words it
surfaces make sense for accounts you know. A row with fewer than eight
words belongs to an account too thinly represented to have eight words
used at least three times. And if a row looks nothing like the account
you know, go back to the language table in Section 1.2: a filter that
silently drops most of an account's posts leaves a caricature of it.
(This is the smoothed log-odds of Monroe, Colaresi, & Quinn 2008.)

## 4. Sentiment analysis with a lexicon

**Dictionary methods** score documents by looking words up in a curated
lexicon. Python uses VADER (Hutto & Gilbert 2014), a lexicon built for
microblog text whose rules also read capitalization, exclamation points,
intensifiers, emoticons and simple negation. tidytext ships the **Bing**
lexicon (Hu & Liu 2004): two plain word lists, positive and negative. Our
score is positive words minus negative words, so it is an integer with no
fixed range, where Python's VADER compound score runs from −1 to +1. The
mechanics differ; the failure modes are the same family. Sentiment gets
the **raw text**, because preprocessing is method-specific: what is noise
to a topic model can be signal to a lexicon. The demos show what
lexicon-based scoring can and cannot see:

```{r sentiment-demo}
score_text <- function(texts) {
  scores <- tibble(doc = seq_along(texts), text = texts) |>
    unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
    inner_join(get_sentiments("bing"), by = "word") |>
    mutate(value = if_else(sentiment == "positive", 1L, -1L)) |>
    group_by(doc) |>
    summarise(score = sum(value))
  tibble(doc = seq_along(texts)) |>
    left_join(scores, by = "doc") |>
    mutate(score = coalesce(score, 0L)) |>
    pull(score)
}

demos <- c("The new feature is good.",
           "The new feature is GOOD!!!",          # emphasis: Bing ignores it
           "The new feature is not good.",        # negation: NOT handled by Bing
           "The new feature is good :(",          # emoticon: not in Bing
           "Oh great, ANOTHER outage. Just what I needed today.")  # sarcasm: no

tibble(text = demos, score = score_text(demos))
```

Note the failures. Unlike VADER, a plain word list scores emphasis,
negation and emoticons exactly like the bare word, so "not good" counts as
positive; and no lexicon catches the sarcasm in the last line. Keep that
in mind whenever you see an aggregate sentiment number. Validation
(Section 7) is not optional. Now score every post and look at the shape
of the distribution. Predict one feature first: a post containing no
lexicon words at all scores exactly 0.

```{r sentiment-corpus, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
corpus <- corpus |> mutate(sentiment = score_text(text))

ggplot(corpus, aes(sentiment)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "mediumpurple", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Bing sentiment score (positive − negative words)",
       y = "Number of posts",
       title = "Sentiment distribution across the corpus") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The big spike at zero is typical of short text: many posts contain no
lexicon words at all, so they score neutral by default. "Neutral" here
often means "no evidence," not "measured neutrality."

### 4.1 Sentiment over time

O'Connor *et al.* (2010) aggregated tweet sentiment into time series and
found it tracked national polls, the founding demonstration that cheap
text measures can proxy expensive surveys. At our small scale we can do
the descriptive version: the monthly mean score with a 95% confidence
band (mean ± 1.96 standard errors), skipping months with fewer than 20
posts.

```{r sentiment-time, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
corpus |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(created_at, "month")) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  filter(n() >= 20) |>
  summarise(mean_sent = mean(sentiment),
            se = sd(sentiment) / sqrt(n())) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, mean_sent)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_sent - 1.96 * se,
                  ymax = mean_sent + 1.96 * se),
              fill = "seagreen", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(color = "seagreen") + geom_point(color = "seagreen") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Mean sentiment score",
       title = "Monthly mean sentiment across the panel corpus") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Treat the monthly line as a demonstration, not a finding. The newsroom
posts dozens of times a day, so its 600 posts cover only the last few
weeks; the earliest months contain only the slower-posting accounts. A
dip or spike in an early month may describe one columnist rather than
the panel, so check how many posts each month rests on before reading
anything into it.

### 4.2 Where dictionaries break

Every dictionary inherits three structural weaknesses:

* **Negation and scope.** VADER catches "not good" but longer-range
  negation ("I wish I could say this was good") slips through; Bing
  catches neither.
* **Sarcasm and irony.** As demonstrated above; communities with heavily
  ironic registers can invert the measure entirely.
* **Domain drift.** Lexicon ratings are frozen at collection time, on the
  platforms and slang of that moment. "Sick" as praise, community
  in-jokes, or political terms whose valence flips over time all decay a
  dictionary's validity.

The remedy is not a better dictionary but a validation habit, starting
with reading the extremes. We display verbatim posts **only from the seed
account** (`nytimes.com`, a large institutional account publishing for a
public audience); for the other panel accounts we report aggregates and
would paraphrase rather than quote, because verbatim text is trivially
re-identifiable via search:

```{r sentiment-extremes}
corpus |>
  filter(author == SEED_ACCOUNT) |>
  arrange(sentiment) |>
  slice(c(1:3, (n() - 2):n())) |>
  transmute(sentiment, text = str_trunc(text, 120))
```

Ask what the extremes are measuring. In a newsroom's feed the most
"positive" posts are often recipes and lifestyle pieces, and the most
"negative" are often straight reporting of deaths and violence: the
lexicon scores the words of the story, not the newsroom's attitude
toward it.

## 5. Topic modeling with LDA

Where dictionaries impose categories, **unsupervised** methods discover
them. **Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)** (Blei, Ng, & Jordan 2003)
treats each post as a *mixture* of topics and each topic as a
*distribution over words*, and learns both from word co-occurrence
alone, with no labels. Note the technical meaning of **topic** here:
nothing more than a probability distribution over the vocabulary.
Whether a given distribution corresponds to a human-recognizable theme
is an empirical question, not a guarantee. And LDA was designed for long
documents: 300-character posts give it very little co-occurrence
evidence per document, so expect a couple of crisp topics and a couple
of junk ones. The model wants a
**document-term matrix** (rows = posts, columns = words, cells =
counts), which `cast_dtm()` builds from our tidy token counts. We first
prune the vocabulary at both ends, as the Python notebook does with
`min_df = 5` and `max_df = 0.4`: drop words appearing in fewer than five
posts (they carry almost no co-occurrence information and balloon the
vocabulary) and words appearing in 40% or more of posts (so common they
can't tell topics apart). Then we fix the random seed, because LDA's
fitting is stochastic:

```{r lda}
n_posts <- n_distinct(tokens$uri)

dtm <- tokens |>
  count(uri, word) |>
  group_by(word) |>
  filter(n_distinct(uri) >= 5,               # word in >= 5 posts
         n_distinct(uri) < 0.4 * n_posts) |> # ...and in < 40% of posts
  ungroup() |>
  cast_dtm(uri, word, n)

N_TOPICS <- 8
lda_fit <- LDA(dtm, k = N_TOPICS, control = list(seed = 42))

dtm
```

### 5.1 Reading the topics

A fitted LDA model has two faces, and tidytext exposes each as a tidy
tibble. The **beta** matrix gives each word's probability under each
topic — reading the top-12 words per topic is how humans decide what a
topic "is":

```{r topic-words}
topic_words <- tidy(lda_fit, matrix = "beta") |>
  group_by(topic) |>
  slice_max(beta, n = 12) |>
  summarise(top_words = paste(term, collapse = ", "))

topic_words
```

Read each row and try to name the topic. If you can't, that's
diagnostic data, not a personal failing.

### 5.2 Documents as topic mixtures

The **gamma** matrix is the other face: each post's estimated mixture
over the topics. Here is the single post in the corpus most dominated by
one topic:

```{r gamma}
doc_topics <- tidy(lda_fit, matrix = "gamma")

most_concentrated <- doc_topics |>
  slice_max(gamma, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

corpus |>
  filter(uri == most_concentrated$document) |>
  transmute(text = str_trunc(text, 200),
            dominant_topic = most_concentrated$topic,
            share = round(most_concentrated$gamma, 2))
```

Most short posts are dominated by one or two topics, with the rest of
the mass spread thinly (an artifact of the Dirichlet prior as much as of
the writing).

### 5.3 Topic prevalence by account

Averaging topic shares within each account gives a *topic profile*, the
unsupervised cousin of Section 3.1's distinctive-words table. A heatmap
makes the panel's division of attention legible at a glance: read a row
to see what an account talks about, a column to see who owns a topic.

```{r prevalence, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
doc_topics |>
  left_join(select(corpus, uri, author), by = c(document = "uri")) |>
  group_by(author, topic) |>
  summarise(mean_share = mean(gamma), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(topic), author, fill = mean_share)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_share, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "darkblue") +
  labs(x = "Topic", y = NULL, fill = "Mean share",
       title = "Topic prevalence by account") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 5.4 Choosing k, and other confessions

We set `k = 8` because it produced readable topics for a corpus of this
size, which is to say, we chose it the way most people actually do.
Honest caveats:

* **There is no true k.** Held-out **perplexity** (how surprised the
  fitted model is by documents it never saw; lower is better, and
  topicmodels exposes it as `perplexity()`) can guide the choice, but
  Chang *et al.* (2009) showed perplexity can *anti*-correlate with human
  topic interpretability. Fit several values, read the topics, and report
  the sensitivity (the
  [ldatuning](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ldatuning) package
  automates several metrics).
* **Topics are not concepts.** They are co-occurrence clusters. Two
  themes that share vocabulary merge; one theme discussed in two registers
  splits. Naming topics is an interpretive act you should document.
* **Instability.** Different random seeds yield different topics; fixing
  the seed makes the *document* stable, not the *finding*.
* **Short texts strain LDA.** Common upgrades: pool posts by author or
  by week into pseudo-documents, use biterm topic models, or move to
  embeddings (next section).

An LDA topic enters a paper only after validation: top words, top
*documents*, and a human check that the label fits.

## 6. Beyond word counts: transformer sentence embeddings

Everything above treated documents as bags of words, discarding order,
syntax, and context. The modern alternative is to encode each post as a
dense vector, a **sentence embedding**, using a pretrained transformer
model (Reimers & Gurevych 2019). Posts that *mean* similar things land
near each other in vector space even when they share no vocabulary
("the eagles won" / "philadelphia takes the championship"), which
dissolves much of Section 2. From R the practical routes are the
[text](https://r-text.org/) package (which wraps Hugging Face
transformers via reticulate) or calling a Python encoder directly. The
workflow is the same as the Python notebook's: embed posts, then
cluster, classify, or measure similarity in the embedding space.

```{r embeddings, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("text"); text::textrpp_install()
embeddings <- text::textEmbed(corpus$text[1:3])
dim(embeddings$texts$texts)
```

The trade-off is interpretability: a topic's top words can be printed
and argued about; the hundreds of dimensions of an embedding cannot. For
research that must justify its measures, count-based methods plus
validation remain a defensible, sometimes preferable, choice.

## 7. Validate, validate, validate

Grimmer & Stewart (2013) close their review of text-as-data methods
with a three-word command, **"validate, validate, validate"**, because
every method in this document produces numbers whether or not those
numbers mean anything. The cheapest, highest-value validation is also
the least glamorous: **read a random sample and check**. The chunk below
draws a reproducible random sample of seed-account posts and lays the
automated measures alongside the text. Read each one and ask: does the
sentiment score match your reading? Does the dominant topic's label fit?
Tally your agreement rate; a real project would do this with a few
hundred posts, multiple coders, and a chance-corrected agreement
statistic like Cohen's kappa.

```{r validation-sample}
set.seed(42)
doc_topics |>
  group_by(document) |>
  slice_max(gamma, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(corpus, by = c(document = "uri")) |>
  filter(author == SEED_ACCOUNT) |>
  slice_sample(n = 8) |>
  transmute(sentiment, dominant_topic = topic,
            text = str_trunc(text, 140))
```

You will probably find a few clear mismatches: a sarcastic post scored
positive, a post assigned to a topic by one incidental word. That
experience, not any summary statistic, is what calibrates how much
weight your measures can bear. Hand-coding is the bottleneck of content
analysis, which is why **Part 08** picks up exactly here: using a large
language model as an annotator at scale and validating *it* against a
hand-coded gold sample with formal agreement metrics.

## 8. Saving the corpus and results

Following the series' reproducibility convention, we save the
analysis-ready corpus (with sentiment scores), the topic table, and a
small JSON of collection parameters and dates, so the analyses above can
be re-run from disk without touching the API:

```{r save}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

write_csv(corpus, "data/corpus.csv")
write_csv(topic_words, "data/topic_top_words.csv")
write_json(
  list(collected_on = COLLECTED_ON, seed_account = SEED_ACCOUNT,
       panel_accounts = panel_dids, language_filter = "declared English, or undeclared with English function-word share >= 0.10",
       n_posts_saved = nrow(corpus), lda_topics = N_TOPICS, lda_seed = 42),
  "data/collection_metadata.json", pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)

read_csv("data/corpus.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> nrow()
```

## Ethics and limitations

**Public text is still people's speech.** Most Bluesky users have not
read the protocol docs and may not expect their posts in a research
corpus (Fiesler & Proferes 2018). This document's conventions are
deliberate: verbatim examples come only from the seed account (a
national newsroom whose posts are professional output); for everyone
else we report aggregates (frequency tables, topic shares, monthly
means) and would paraphrase rather than quote, because verbatim posts
are trivially re-identifiable via search (Zimmer 2010). The saved corpus
records its collection date so deletions can be honored if the archive
is ever shared; better still, share derived measures rather than raw
text.

**A mention-based panel is not a sample.** A handful of accounts in one
newsroom's conversational orbit, mostly its own sister accounts and
journalists, support a tutorial, not a population claim. Bluesky's user
base itself skews toward early adopters and Twitter migrants, so even a
good sample of it would not generalize to "the public."

**The English filter has politics.** Self-declared `langs` is sometimes
wrong and often missing, and the missingness follows the software an
account uses, so filtering on it can drop whole accounts without warning
(Section 1.2). Our function-word test recovers undeclared English posts,
but any English-only design still excludes non-English speakers
entirely. A multilingual design needs multilingual tools, and the
embeddings of Section 6 are a start.

**Measures are not meanings.** Lexicons miss sarcasm and drift across
domains; LDA topics are co-occurrence clusters that merge, split, and
shift with the random seed; word counts ignore order and context. Every
number above is a model output, defensible only to the extent it has
been validated against human reading, which is also the bridge to Part
08.

**Behavior under incentives, not attitudes.** Posts measure public
expression on a platform, with its norms and audiences, not private
belief. A panel's sentiment trend tells you how they *post*, not how
they *feel*.

## Exercises

Each exercise extends this document. The first few are small
modifications; the later ones are mini-analyses you could write up in a
page or two.

1. **Change the number of topics.** Re-fit the Section 5 model with
   `N_TOPICS <- 5` and again with `N_TOPICS <- 12`, regenerating the
   top-words table each time. Which of the `k = 8` topics merge at 5, and
   which split at 12? Write one sentence per model saying which value you
   would defend and why.
2. **Add custom stopwords.** Look at the top-20 unigram chart in Section
   3 and pick two or three words that read as corpus-specific filler
   rather than content. Add them to `custom_stop`, then re-run Sections 3
   and 5. How sensitive are the frequency rankings and topics to this
   small change?
3. **Swap the panel.** Re-run Section 1 with `SEED_ACCOUNT <- "bsky.app"`
   and let the mention snowball build a new panel. Compare the
   distinctive-words table and topic heatmap to the originals. What does
   the contrast teach you about how much these measures depend on corpus
   construction rather than on the method?
4. **Bigram topics.** Build the LDA document-term matrix from bigrams
   instead of unigrams and refit. Are the top-words tables easier or
   harder to label? Watch what happens to the vocabulary size, and think
   about why a much larger vocabulary might hurt a model fitted to a
   corpus of very short documents.
5. **Sentiment around an event.** Find a month where the Section 4.1
   trend line dips or spikes. Filter `corpus` to that month, sort by
   `sentiment`, and read the ten most extreme posts (verbatim only for
   the seed account, paraphrase for others). Was the swing driven by a
   real-world event, by a change in *who* was posting, or by a lexicon
   failure mode? Deliver a 3–4 sentence verdict with evidence.
6. **Distinctive terms, head to head.** Adapt Section 3.1 to compare just
   two panel accounts directly, and inspect *both* tails: the largest
   log-odds are distinctively A's vocabulary, the smallest distinctively
   B's. This two-corpus design is exactly the "fightin' words" setting of
   Monroe, Colaresi, & Quinn (2008).

## Research project ideas

**1. How do newsrooms frame the same story differently?** *Question:*
when several news organizations on Bluesky cover the same event, do they
use systematically different vocabularies and emphases? *Data:* a panel
corpus built with Section 1's collector, but with a defensible,
criterion-based panel (say, 10–20 newsroom accounts chosen *before*
looking at their content), restricted to a pre-registered window around
one event. *Method:* distinctive-terms log-odds between outlets (Section
3.1) plus an LDA fitted on the pooled corpus with topic prevalence by
outlet (Section 5.3); have two coders independently label the topics and
a sample of posts, and report a chance-corrected agreement statistic
(Krippendorff 2018). *Expected challenge:* 300-character posts give LDA
very thin co-occurrence evidence, so you will likely need to pool posts
into per-outlet-per-day pseudo-documents, a decision that itself needs
justification and a sensitivity check.

**2. An audit of off-the-shelf sentiment on Bluesky.** *Question:* how
valid are lexicon methods on 2026 Bluesky text, and where exactly do they
fail? Van Atteveldt, van der Velden, & Boukes (2021) ran this design on
Dutch news headlines and found dictionary methods trailing far behind
human coders and trained classifiers; does the same hold here? *Data:* a
few thousand posts from a topical corpus (Part 02's authenticated
search), with a random sample of ~300 posts hand-coded negative, neutral
or positive by two or three coders. *Method:* threshold the lexicon score
into the same three classes and compare against the human gold standard
(accuracy, per-class recall, and a qualitative autopsy of the misses).
*Expected challenge:* the bottleneck is the codebook: if your coders
cannot agree with each other, no instrument can be meaningfully validated
against their labels. This design connects directly to Part 08.

**3. Do network communities talk differently?** *Question:* do the
follow-graph communities detected in Part 03 have measurably distinctive
vocabularies, that is, do structural and linguistic boundaries coincide?
*Data:* community assignments from a Part 03 collection, plus
author-feed corpora for the accounts in the two or three largest
communities. *Method:* distinctive-terms analysis and topic prevalence by
community, then a simple bag-of-words classifier predicting community
membership; validate by reading the highest- and lowest-confidence
predictions. *Expected challenge:* communities differ in many correlated
ways at once (topic, register, geography), so the interesting work is
disentangling *why* the text is classifiable, not just reporting that it
is.
